title: Boundary Layers, Displacement Flow, and the High-Frequency Response of Porous Media: Beyond the Viscous and Thermal Characteristic Lengths, Order by Order
authors: D. Lafarge, A. Bouchendouka, Z. E. A. Fellah
abstract: The Johnson-Koplik-Dashen viscous characteristic length $Λ$ and its thermal analogue $Λ'$ introduced by Champoux and Allard govern the leading $O(ω^{-1/2})$ boundary-layer behaviour of fluid-saturated porous media, but omit higher microgeometric effects associated with interface curvature and field gradients. We develop the asymptotic high-frequency expansions of dynamic tortuosity and dynamic compressibility beyond the leading boundary-layer terms. By resolving the oscillatory Stokes and heat conduction problems in the thin boundary-layer limit, we establish a recursive hierarchy, which can be continued to any order, defining successive microgeometric parameters, given by wall integrals. Each order requires transport equations of WKB type across the boundary layer, closed by a non-secularity condition, together with one Neumann problem for the potential displacement flow that the boundary layer induces. Applied to the values fitted on highly absorbing foams, these expressions show that the negative surface parameter is consistent with strong in-parallel disorder of the pore sizes, whereas the large positive third-order term points to strong constrictions or enlargements along part of the flow paths. The thermal parameters reduce to geometrical quantities: the integral mean curvature of the pore walls, a Willmore-type measure of their departure from umbilicity and, at the next order, this measure weighted by the mean curvature. Using the Avellaneda-Torquato relaxation-mode representation, we show that all these parameters are spectral data of the distribution of relaxation times. For isolated sharp edges across which the fluid flows, the singular terms of the formal expansion cancel, and the description persists with apparent, logarithmically varying values of the parameters.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive high-frequency expansion extends porous-media response beyond viscous and thermal characteristic lengths, capturing curvature, field gradients, and boundary-layer-induced displacement flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps interpret acoustic response in porous absorbers by linking higher-order coefficients to pore-size disorder and flow-path constrictions or enlargements.
method: Resolve oscillatory Stokes flow and heat conduction in thin boundary layers.
Combine WKB-type transport equations, non-secularity conditions, and a displacement-flow Neumann problem at each order.
Express successive coefficients through wall integrals and relaxation-time spectral data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Applying the expressions to coefficients fitted for highly absorbing foams links a negative surface parameter to in-parallel pore-size disorder and a large positive third-order term to flow-path constrictions or enlargements.
infographic.watch_item: The expansion is a high-frequency asymptotic description; isolated sharp edges require apparent, logarithmically varying parameters rather than fixed coefficients.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary Layers, Displacement Flow, and the High-Frequency Response of Porous Media: Beyond the Viscous and Thermal Characteristic Lengths, Order by Order

title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
authors: Louenas Zemmour, Xavier Gloerfelt, Paola Cinnella
abstract: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$ω$-$γ$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

infographic.key_insight: CFD-driven symbolic regression learns compact, interpretable corrections to a RANS transition model that improve predictions beyond the flat-plate training cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate transition modeling can improve turbomachinery heat-transfer and loss predictions, with heat-transfer errors reduced by up to 70% in tested turbine-cascade conditions.
method: Correct intermittency production and destruction activation functions using pressure-gradient polynomials and bounded exponentials of local flow features.
Fit coefficients with gradient-free, RANS-in-the-loop optimization accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates.
Select elastic-net hyperparameters through bi-level optimization and leave-one-case-out cross-validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on wall-resolved LES mean velocities for ERCOFTAC T3 flat plates, the model retained 11 of 21 candidate terms and improved heat-transfer predictions at all four unseen LS89 turbine-cascade operating points without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Residual errors in transition onset and length indicate that flat-plate-only training limits predictive accuracy in more complex flows.
infographic.paper_title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models

title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework
authors: David Gabriel Harispe, Matías Gerard, Pablo A. Kler
abstract: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.

infographic.key_insight: Uncertainty-guided simulation enrichment improves neural-network surrogates for microdroplet generation and supports confidence-aware inverse design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces reliance on costly multiphase-flow simulations when designing microfluidic devices for target droplet sizes.
method: Train neural-network ensembles on high-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations to predict flow regimes and droplet diameters.
Use regime consensus and diameter coefficient of variation to target additional simulations near uncertain transitions and address class imbalance.
Apply Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing target accuracy, predictive confidence, and physical consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: On independent test datasets, enrichment nearly doubled the fraction of diameter predictions with 0–3% error and substantially reduced cases above 10% error.
infographic.watch_item: Ensemble agreement does not guarantee accuracy outside the simulated parameter space; new operating conditions may require additional high-fidelity validation.
infographic.paper_title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework

title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
authors: Nicolas Tricard, Linzheng Wang, Jason Chen, Sili Deng
abstract: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.

infographic.key_insight: No reconstruction method wins across all flow regimes: classical estimators remain competitive, while learned models gain an advantage as sensor density or observability decreases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sparse-sensor flow reconstruction should be selected for the flow regime, measured variables, uncertainty needs and computational budget rather than accuracy alone.
method: Compare 10 learned and 5 classical methods across cylinder-wake, 2D Kolmogorov and 3D isotropic flows.
Use shared leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws.
Evaluate per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and computational cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical methods lead on the cylinder wake, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed 3D channels, and Kolmogorov rankings differ between pointwise error and probabilistic scoring.
infographic.watch_item: Generative ensembles remain underdispersed; larger sampler budgets improve ensemble quality at higher cost, while full-grid construction methods can exhaust memory at scale.
infographic.paper_title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

title: A coupled lattice Boltzmann model for pore-scale mushy-layer dynamics with application to sea ice
authors: Nicola Trippella, Dario Maggiolo
abstract: A pore-scale lattice Boltzmann model is developed for reactive transport in phase-changing porous media, coupling solute transport in the liquid with conjugate heat transfer across the solid and liquid phases. Two methodological developments are introduced: a novel link-based Volume-of-Pixel formulation for direction-dependent interface motion, and a generalized Robin boundary treatment for solute redistribution at moving interfaces. The phase-change formulation is validated against thermal benchmarks, while the Robin treatment is assessed through literature test cases, exhibiting convergence rates between first and second order. The coupled model is then applied to a local pore-scale segment of a sea ice brine channel in a purely diffusive regime. The simulations recover the expected ideal mushy-layer behaviour under appropriate scale separation. At sea-ice-relevant concentration ratios, thermal perturbations produce relatively large variations in brine salinity, causing freezing rather than melting to reshape the pore geometry in a non-uniform way. The resulting framework provides a pore-scale numerical tool for resolving coupled temperature, solute redistribution, and phase-boundary dynamics in mushy layers.

infographic.key_insight: A coupled pore-scale lattice Boltzmann model shows how thermal perturbations can drive salinity changes and non-uniform freezing in sea-ice brine channels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports detailed simulation of heat transfer, solute redistribution, and evolving pore geometry in phase-changing porous materials.
method: Couple liquid solute transport with conjugate solid–liquid heat transfer.
Track direction-dependent interface motion using a link-based Volume-of-Pixel formulation.
Treat solute redistribution at moving interfaces with a generalized Robin boundary condition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Thermal benchmarks validate phase change, literature tests show first- to second-order convergence for the Robin treatment, and diffusive brine-channel simulations recover ideal mushy-layer behaviour under appropriate scale separation.
infographic.watch_item: The sea-ice application is local and purely diffusive; performance with advective transport or larger-scale channel networks is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A coupled lattice Boltzmann model for pore-scale mushy-layer dynamics with application to sea ice

title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device
authors: Luciano Hergenreder, Serge Simoëns, Cristián Escauriaza, Wernher Brevis
abstract: We investigate the interscale energy dynamics of nearly homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) generated in a spherically forced, propeller-driven device. From a spatial perspective, by employing the Kármán-Howarth-Monin (KHM) framework, we analyze the scale-by-scale energy transfer without isotropy assumptions. In contrast to other forcing strategies, where regions with inverse and forward cascades often coexist in scale space, we show that spherical forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across the entire scale space. While the energy distribution remains highly isotropic and orientation-averaged structure functions align with Kolmogorov's two-thirds law, the energy flux exhibits a directional dependence, suggesting a higher sensitivity to residual forcing asymmetries. Regarding the temporal dynamics, the reduced mean flow generated by this device allows us to investigate the temporal variability in conditions where Taylor's frozen turbulence hypothesis does not apply. Our results provide experimental validation of Tennekes' Eulerian frequency spectrum, where intermediate scales evidence an inertial-convective range with statistics determined by the integral velocity scale and the dissipation rate. Finally, we adopt a global approach to investigate whether the main turbulent scales can be linked to external experimental parameters. We propose a framework that captures the propeller frequency dependence of the main turbulent variables obtained in our measurements and those of previously reported HIT chambers. These findings contribute to the understanding of how external forcing influences the complex interscale energy dynamics of turbulent flows from a spatial, temporal, and global perspective.

infographic.key_insight: Spherical propeller forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across the analyzed scales, while energy flux remains direction-dependent despite nearly isotropic energy statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings inform the design and operation of turbulence chambers by linking forcing geometry and propeller frequency to turbulent energy transfer and key flow scales.
method: Apply the Kármán–Howarth–Monin framework without assuming isotropy.
Analyze temporal fluctuations under low-mean-flow conditions where Taylor’s frozen-turbulence hypothesis does not apply.
Develop a propeller-frequency scaling framework using measurements from this device and previously reported HIT chambers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements show orientation-averaged structure functions consistent with Kolmogorov’s two-thirds law and an intermediate-scale Eulerian frequency spectrum supporting Tennekes’ prediction.
infographic.watch_item: Nearly isotropic energy statistics do not guarantee isotropic energy transfer; residual forcing asymmetries can remain visible in directional flux.
infographic.paper_title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
authors: Semih Kacmaz, E. A. Huerta
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

infographic.key_insight: Learned UNet and transformer surrogates emulate 3D resistive MHD turbulence with relative velocity errors of 0.018–0.053 while preserving key flow structures and statistics over about one large-eddy turnover time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These surrogates offer a potential route to faster plasma-flow modeling for astrophysics and fusion, though deployment speedups are not quantified in the abstract.
method: Compare a convolutional UNet, shifted-window transformer and Fourier neural operator as autoregressive emulators.
Train on 128³ decaying MHD simulations at Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000.
Use single-step training followed by short-rollout training, with a common stopping rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training uses 500 simulations per Reynolds number; public-benchmark evaluations report 39% lower error than the best published FactFormer isotropic-turbulence model and one-third to one-half lower rollout errors than the best baselines on The Well's compressible MHD set.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the reported rollout windows and generalization to other MHD regimes remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence

title: A physics-informed neural network method for pressure-driven turbine-blade optimization
authors: Yuan Huang, Francesca di Mare
abstract: We develop a physics-informed method for aerodynamic shape optimisation of turbine blades, treating the flow field and blade geometry as coupled unknowns. The method translates prescribed surface-pressure distributions into geometric modifications through pressure-target continuation and alternating flow-geometry updates. A differentiable representation of the blade surfaces allows their positions and orientations to be optimised within the current flow field, followed by flow re-adaptation to the modified boundaries. The inverse formulation uses the two-dimensional steady compressible Euler equations as physics constraints and is evaluated on the LS89 turbine cascade using 28 pressure-target points derived from experimental data. Starting from a modified profile and a warm-started flow network, the final pressure-side and suction-side root-mean-square fitting errors are 1.13% and 2.21% of inlet total pressure, respectively. Independent forward verification with SharC reproduces the principal surface-pressure trends of the experimental measurements, with remaining differences near the trailing edge. These results demonstrate the translation of experimental-origin loading data into geometric blade modifications through coordinated optimisation of the flow field and moving boundaries.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network jointly updates turbine-blade geometry and flow to match prescribed surface-pressure targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a route from experimentally derived blade-loading targets to aerodynamic shape modifications.
method: Constrain the flow with the 2D steady compressible Euler equations.
Use pressure-target continuation and differentiable blade surfaces to update geometry.
Alternate geometry optimisation with flow re-adaptation to moving boundaries.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the LS89 cascade with 28 experimental-derived pressure targets, final pressure-side and suction-side RMSEs were 1.13% and 2.21% of inlet total pressure; independent SharC verification reproduced the main pressure trends.
infographic.watch_item: The evaluation uses a 2D inviscid formulation and a warm-started flow network, with remaining pressure discrepancies near the trailing edge.
infographic.paper_title: A physics-informed neural network method for pressure-driven turbine-blade optimization

title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies
authors: Flavio Tuteri, André Freitas
abstract: Turbulence is defined by a set of emergent and singular phenomena: a constant-flux energy cascade, intermittency, a dissipation rate that survives the vanishing of viscosity, and the spontaneous loss of determinism of the inviscid limit. Which physical ingredients produce them remains unclear, because in fluids they always come together with incompressibility, spatial structure and vortex dynamics. Here we show that a hierarchy of inertia, coupled by the purely geometric nonlinearity of rigid constraints, is enough. A planar chain of rigid pendula whose lengths and masses decrease geometrically, coupled only through nearest-neighbor constraints, develops a far-from-equilibrium cascade that replaces thermal equipartition, with statistically local and time-irreversible energy transfer despite intrinsically nonlocal coupling. Its fluctuations are intermittent, yet self-similarity is restored by a hidden scale symmetry. As the viscosity vanishes, the dissipation rate saturates at a finite value, and thermal noise consistent with fluctuation-dissipation balance is amplified from the smallest to the largest scales within a fraction of a large-scale period. Because the hierarchy can be tuned and the same dynamics can be realized mechanically or electrically, turbulence becomes a property that can be designed and measured in the laboratory.

infographic.key_insight: A hierarchy of rigid pendula reproduces hallmark turbulence phenomena through inertia and geometric constraints, without fluid incompressibility or vortex dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tunable mechanical or electrical realizations could provide controlled laboratory platforms for designing and measuring turbulence-like energy transfer.
method: Use a planar chain of rigid pendula with geometrically decreasing lengths and masses.
Couple neighboring pendula through rigid constraints to generate nonlinear dynamics.
Examine energy transfer, intermittency, dissipation and thermal-noise amplification as viscosity decreases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports statistically local, irreversible energy transfer, intermittent fluctuations, finite dissipation as viscosity vanishes, and noise amplification across scales within a fraction of a large-scale period.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation details or demonstrated hardware implementation, so experimental robustness remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies

title: Experimental evaluation of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis for shear-dependent viscosity fluids
authors: Luciano Hergenreder, Serge Simoëns, Wernher Brevis
abstract: We experimentally investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis to shear-dependent viscosity fluids. We assess whether dissipative range statistics exhibit a self-similar behavior in nearly homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, using stereo particle image velocimetry in aqueous Carbopol solutions across two concentrations and a range of forcing conditions. We observe that, when normalized by the mean viscosity and mean dissipation rate, second- and third-order structure functions collapse across the different experimental conditions and exhibit functional forms compatible with classical Newtonian results. These observations are in general agreement with the recent numerical results of Rosti [J. Fluid Mech. 1012, R5 (2025)], who proposed that Kolmogorov's similarity hypotheses can be extended to shear-thinning fluids by considering dissipation scales based on the mean viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the flow index.

infographic.key_insight: Dissipative-range turbulence statistics in shear-dependent viscosity fluids show self-similar behavior consistent with extending Kolmogorov’s first similarity hypothesis beyond Newtonian fluids.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings support mean-viscosity-based scaling for interpreting small-scale turbulence in shear-thinning fluid systems.
method: Generate nearly homogeneous, isotropic turbulence in aqueous Carbopol solutions.
Use stereo particle image velocimetry at two concentrations and multiple forcing conditions.
Normalize second- and third-order structure functions using mean viscosity and mean dissipation rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Normalized structure functions collapse across experimental conditions and exhibit forms compatible with classical Newtonian results, broadly agreeing with recent numerical findings.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the tested Carbopol solutions and flow conditions; applicability to other rheologies or strongly anisotropic flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental evaluation of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis for shear-dependent viscosity fluids

title: A Drift-Diffusion Approach for Pearson Type IV Heavy-Tail Distributions
authors: Daniele Belardinelli, Simone Benella, Mirko Stumpo, Giuseppe Consolini
abstract: Non-Gaussian stationary fluctuations with heavy tails and finite-order moment cutoffs are ubiquitous in non-equilibrium systems. Here, we derive the Pearson type IV distribution as the stationary solution of a standardized Fokker-Planck equation with linear drift and quadratic diffusion. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for its emergence and show that the linear-quadratic structure, although sufficient, is not necessary. We also give explicit closed expressions for the cumulative distribution function, a moment recurrence relation, skewness, kurtosis, and mode. From a physical perspective, our results reveal that heavy tails and asymmetry originate from distinct features of state-dependent diffusion: its local nonlinear curvature and gradient, respectively. In particular, asymmetric stationary fluctuations can emerge even in the presence of a symmetric linear restoring drift. This framework provides a general stochastic description of asymmetric heavy-tailed fluctuations in non-equilibrium systems, including space plasma turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Pearson type IV heavy-tailed, asymmetric fluctuations can arise from state-dependent diffusion even with a symmetric linear restoring drift.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a stochastic basis for modeling asymmetric, extreme fluctuations in non-equilibrium flows and space plasma turbulence.
method: Derive Pearson type IV stationary distributions from linear-drift, quadratic-diffusion Fokker–Planck dynamics.
Establish necessary and sufficient emergence conditions beyond the linear–quadratic construction.
Obtain closed-form distribution statistics and a moment recurrence relation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations, linking heavy tails to diffusion curvature and asymmetry to its gradient, but describes no empirical or numerical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Check which moments exist before using skewness or kurtosis, since heavy tails impose finite-order moment cutoffs.
infographic.paper_title: A Drift-Diffusion Approach for Pearson Type IV Heavy-Tail Distributions

title: Fluid memory beyond creeping flow: a history kernel for a sphere at finite Reynolds numbers
authors: M. D. Łasica, J. G. M. Kuerten, S. K. F. Stoter
abstract: Predicting the history force on a sphere beyond the creeping-flow limit remains challenging. Existing formulations have been derived or calibrated for selected flow histories, with limited evidence of their predictive accuracy under more general conditions. We develop a systematic approach to extract the history kernel of a fixed sphere in spatially uniform, unsteady flow from axisymmetric Navier-Stokes simulations of finite-duration acceleration and deceleration ramps at initial Reynolds numbers from 0.2 to 200. The resulting kernel surface recovers the Basset limit at short lags and in the creeping-flow limit and is continued beyond the resolved lags using far-wake asymptotics. At higher Reynolds numbers, the kernel develops non-monotonic behaviour at intermediate lags, associated with delayed adjustment of the boundary layer and wake. For the cases tested, the present kernel substantially improves history-force predictions for finite ramps, oscillatory forcing and non-periodic composite velocity histories relative to the literature formulations considered, without case-specific adjustment. These findings indicate that lag and Reynolds number capture the dominant memory response.

infographic.key_insight: A history kernel indexed by time lag and Reynolds number captures sphere-flow memory beyond creeping flow, including non-monotonic responses at higher Reynolds numbers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The kernel can improve transient hydrodynamic-force predictions for spheres when finite-Reynolds-number fluid memory matters.
method: Extract kernels from axisymmetric Navier–Stokes simulations of finite acceleration and deceleration ramps.
Cover initial Reynolds numbers from 0.2 to 200 while recovering the short-lag and creeping-flow Basset limits.
Extend beyond resolved time lags using far-wake asymptotics.
infographic.evidence_signal: For tested ramps, oscillatory forcing and non-periodic composite velocity histories, the kernel substantially improved history-force predictions over the literature formulations considered without case-specific adjustment.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the tested fixed-sphere, spatially uniform, axisymmetric flow conditions; broader applicability requires further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Fluid memory beyond creeping flow: a history kernel for a sphere at finite Reynolds numbers

title: On the role of grazing atmospheric particles in hypersonic boundary-layer receptivity
authors: Sean Dungan, Christoph Brehm
abstract: The role of small atmospheric particulates in the initiation of the laminar-turbulent transition is investigated for the HIFLIER vehicle during Mach 6 ascent condition. High-fidelity simulations are used to examine the disturbance wavepackets generated by particles following either grazing trajectories through the boundary layer or trajectories that lead to impact and rebound at the cone surface. Grazing particles that penetrate less than halfway through the boundary layer are found to generate wavepackets with amplitudes comparable to those produced by wall-impinging particles. To identify the receptivity mechanisms responsible for this behaviour, a multiple-scales asymptotic formulation is developed that accounts for the extended streamwise region over which a particle interacts with the boundary layer. The analysis shows that a grazing particle can generate a strong disturbance response when crossing the critical layer, where the streamwise-momentum component of the adjoint mode is largest and the boundary layer is most receptive. Thus, direct surface impact is not required for atmospheric particulates to excite dynamically significant instability waves. Root-mean-square disturbance estimates for submicron grazing particles predict transition-onset locations close to those measured in flight, suggesting they may have contributed significantly to the onset of transition on HIFLIER at the trajectory condition considered.

infographic.key_insight: At Mach 6, grazing atmospheric particles can excite strong hypersonic boundary-layer instability waves without hitting the surface by crossing the highly receptive critical layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for grazing particulates could improve transition-onset predictions for hypersonic vehicles.
method: High-fidelity simulations of grazing and impact–rebound particle trajectories on HIFLIER.
Multiple-scales asymptotic analysis of extended particle–boundary-layer interactions.
Root-mean-square disturbance estimates for submicron grazing particles.
infographic.evidence_signal: Particles penetrating less than halfway through the boundary layer produced wavepacket amplitudes comparable to wall-impinging particles, while estimated transition-onset locations were close to flight measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement at the studied Mach 6 ascent condition suggests a particulate contribution but does not establish causation or applicability across flight conditions.
infographic.paper_title: On the role of grazing atmospheric particles in hypersonic boundary-layer receptivity

title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations
authors: Manvendra Modgil
abstract: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.

infographic.key_insight: Fluid properties can be readable from learned latents without being controllable through them; strong decoding does not guarantee useful steering.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controllable fluid surrogates should be evaluated by how latent interventions change decoded flows, not just by how accurately latents predict physical quantities.
method: Tested JEPA representations of 2D decaying Navier–Stokes flow against untrained, non-physical-dynamics and static-invariance controls.
Compared plain autoencoders with VICReg-regularized models for enstrophy prominence and linear decodability.
Routed overall scale through a small conditioning code and degraded spectral shape through a separate pathway to build output-steering dials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three pre-registered studies were tested once on held-out data: JEPA's claimed advantage was unsupported, autoencoder enstrophy correlations reached 0.80–0.86 versus 0.38 untrained, and shape steering succeeded in 3 of 5 fresh seeds, below the required 4.
infographic.watch_item: Shape steering remained seed-sensitive, and results on 2D decaying flow do not establish reliable control in broader turbulence settings.
infographic.paper_title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations

title: Lagrangian Irreversibility in Stratified Turbulence
authors: Mrinal Jyoti Powdel, Samriddhi Sankar Ray
abstract: Stable stratification reorganizes turbulence, suppressing vertical motion and altering the balance between vortical and strain-dominated flow structures. How these changes affect the temporal asymmetry of kinetic-energy exchange along fluid-particle trajectories remains incompletely understood. Using direct numerical simulations of homogeneous Boussinesq turbulence, we investigate Lagrangian power statistics across four local velocity-gradient topology classes and three nonzero stratification strengths, with an unstratified reference case. With increasing stratification, the global power variance decreases while the standardized skewness becomes more negative, indicating enhanced asymmetry despite weaker fluctuations. Conditioning on local topology reveals distinct responses: axial-strain-dominated regions exhibit the most negative total-power skewness at all stratification strengths, whereas biaxial-strain-dominated regions change sign from positive to negative under stratification. Horizontal and vertical component powers also respond differently, revealing directional dependence. Among the dynamical contributions to power, the pressure contribution, nearly symmetric in the unstratified case, becomes more negatively skewed with increasing stratification. Energy-conditioned pressure statistics further indicate altered pressure-mediated energy redistribution. Finally, tracer persistence-time distributions exhibit exponential tails, with time scales that differ across topology classes and respond differently to stratification. Increasing stratification is thus accompanied by three concurrent changes: enhanced asymmetry of Lagrangian power, modified energy redistribution by pressure, and altered temporal sampling of local flow structures by tracers. These co-occurring signatures characterize the response to stratification, though their causal relations remain to be established.

infographic.key_insight: Stronger stable stratification weakens Lagrangian power fluctuations yet increases their negative skewness, revealing greater temporal asymmetry in particle-level kinetic-energy exchange.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results can inform assessment of turbulence models for stratified flows by highlighting topology-dependent and directional differences in energy exchange.
method: Direct numerical simulations of homogeneous Boussinesq turbulence.
Three nonzero stratification strengths compared with an unstratified reference.
Topology-conditioned power, pressure redistribution, and tracer persistence statistics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show decreasing global power variance, increasingly negative standardized skewness, and exponential tracer-persistence tails with topology-dependent time scales.
infographic.watch_item: The causal links among power asymmetry, pressure-mediated redistribution, and altered tracer sampling remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Lagrangian Irreversibility in Stratified Turbulence

title: Transitional Fluid-Ablation Interactions on a Compression Ramp at Mach 8
authors: Ata Onur Başkaya, Sean Dungan, Stefan Hickel, Christoph Brehm
abstract: Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed for a Mach 8 flow over a 15 degree compression ramp undergoing ablation to analyze fluid-ablation interaction (FAI) effects on instability growth and transition of the high-speed boundary layer. Wind-tunnel experiments at these conditions show characteristic heating streaks which are first replicated for laminar flow over an inert ramp. Perturbations superimposed on the laminar baseflow are informed by stability calculations. The ramp is then replaced by a low-temperature ablator in our DNS and the interaction of the streaks with the ablating surface is examined. Ablation models implemented in two independently-developed fluid dynamics solvers are used to study this problem. Overall, both solvers have shown an excellent agreement regarding heat fluxes, mass blowing rates, and recession patterns. Numerical experiments are performed to assess the impact of accelerating recession and of higher amplitude perturbations. We demonstrate accurate predictions of ablative recession and present novel findings regarding its influence on the perturbation evolution for this configuration.

infographic.key_insight: Mach 8 compression-ramp simulations show that ablation interacts with boundary-layer streaks and influences perturbation evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting coupled surface recession and boundary-layer instability can support thermal-protection design for hypersonic vehicles.
method: Direct numerical simulation of Mach 8 flow over a 15° compression ramp.
Stability-informed perturbations applied to inert and low-temperature ablating surfaces.
Two independent solvers tested accelerated recession and higher-amplitude perturbations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations reproduced characteristic experimental heating streaks on an inert ramp, while both solvers showed excellent agreement in heat fluxes, mass blowing rates, and recession patterns.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish experimental validation of the coupled ablating-flow predictions or applicability beyond this configuration.
infographic.paper_title: Transitional Fluid-Ablation Interactions on a Compression Ramp at Mach 8

title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions
authors: Sandesh Lamsal, Sumit Kumar, Rubi Bhandari, Subhamoy Sen, Andrzej Rutkiewicz, Leszek Małyszko
abstract: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks identify tensegrity prestress across taut–slack transitions, which can reveal member parameters that taut-only records leave undetermined.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports prestress monitoring in tensegrity structures, where tension loss can alter stability, stiffness, and dynamic response.
method: Train networks on equation-of-motion residuals in constrained Cartesian coordinates.
Jointly identify force densities, damping, and axial stiffness while retaining tension-only cable behavior.
Use Fisher-information analysis before inversion to assess parameter identifiability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on simulated frames and a 3D prism plus two measured systems yielded force-density errors within 1.5% for identifiable one-module parameters, 4.2% median error for five modules, and 2.9% RMS agreement with measured simplex prestress.
infographic.watch_item: Parameter recovery depends on sensor coverage and excitation; check identifiability before interpreting estimates for individual members.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions

title: Finite-time mixing and reaction in packed bed reactors
authors: Dario Maggiolo, Lucien Magson, Gunther Munz, Diego Sampedro, Angela Sasic Kalagasidis
abstract: We investigate mixing dynamics in porous media at finite times, using pore-scale lattice-Boltzmann simulations combined with Lagrangian particle tracking. We compute fluid deformation in randomly packed beds based on the moving Protean frame approach introduced by Lester 2018. From the extracted Lagrangian kinematics, we construct a mixing model based on lamellar aggregation that well predicts the Eulerian scalar fields obtained from simulations. Our results reveal an early time mixing regime dominated by shear-driven fluid deformation, where solute mixing arises from the random overlap of diffusive concentration elements. In this regime, mixing proceeds slowly and follows a temporal decay of concentration variance, $σ_c^2 \sim Pe^{-α/(2α+1)} t^{-1/2}$, where Pe is the Peclet number and $α$ the exponent characterizing shear deformation. This dynamic arises when the Peclet number is small relative to the ratio between the exponential-mixing and shear-deformation timescales. This analysis also demonstrates that shear-induced mixing govern the homogenization of early-stage reactions at the fluid-solid interface in finite-size random packed beds, typically operating at moderate Peclet numbers $Pe =O(10^2)$.

infographic.key_insight: Early-time mixing in random packed beds is dominated by shear-driven deformation and random overlap of diffusing solute elements, yielding slow concentration-variance decay proportional to t^(-1/2).
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shear-induced mixing governs early-stage homogenization of fluid–solid interface reactions in finite packed beds operating at moderate Peclet numbers, Pe = O(10^2).
method: Pore-scale lattice-Boltzmann simulations with Lagrangian particle tracking.
Moving Protean frame analysis to quantify fluid deformation.
Lamellar aggregation model built from Lagrangian kinematics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The lamellar aggregation model predicts simulated Eulerian scalar fields well, with early-time variance scaling as σ_c² ∼ Pe^[-α/(2α+1)] t^(-1/2), where α characterizes shear deformation.
infographic.watch_item: The shear-dominated scaling applies to an early-time regime under a Peclet-number condition tied to competing deformation timescales; it should not be assumed valid at all times or flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-time mixing and reaction in packed bed reactors

title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
authors: Miranda J S Horne, Peter K Jimack, Amirul Khan, He Wang
abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

infographic.key_insight: Adding a fixed hard-constraint projection layer to a PINN enforces a local discrete Burgers’ equation constraint and improves accuracy over a comparable PINN.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hard constraint projection could improve physics consistency and reduce sensitivity to collocation-point selection in neural fluid-flow solvers.
method: Locally discretise the nonlinear 1D Burgers’ equation using a finite-difference stencil.
Decompose the discrete equation into constraint and prediction matrices to construct a projection.
Project PINN velocity predictions onto the discrete constraint hyperplane using a non-trainable final layer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Initial tests on an unseen uniform grid showed approximately an order-of-magnitude lower data error than a comparable PINN, alongside better governing-equation adherence.
infographic.watch_item: Exact enforcement applies to the local discrete constraint, not the continuous PDE; results are preliminary and limited to 1D Burgers’ equation.
infographic.paper_title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)

title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface
authors: Mohammad Jannesari, Francesco Costanzo
abstract: This paper extends our prior work on interface conditions between two poroelastic domains to the case when a poroelastic domain interacts with a pure fluid. The porous medium is assumed to be deformable and modeled following mixture theory. When not in a mixture, each constituent of the porous domain is assumed to be incompressible. An arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian formulation is developed for both the fluid and porous domains. The fluid velocity and pressure fields are allowed to be discontinuous across the pure fluid/porous domain interface. A globally continuous displacement field is defined to represent both the deformation of the solid skeleton of the poroelastic medium and the mesh motion in the pure fluid domain. As an interface condition, the continuity of the normal component of the filtration velocity is enforced via a Lagrange multiplier. The mixture momentum jump condition is implemented so as to transfer the traction from the fluid side to the porous domain. A dissipative behavior is attributed to the interface, and the jump condition for the fluid momentum, derived from Hamilton's principle, incorporates this prescribed behavior. The model implementation is verified using the method of manufactured solutions, and a sample problem is solved to compare an inert interface with a fully dissipative one. The results show satisfactory convergence rates, while the proposed model successfully reproduces the analytical solution of a benchmark problem using conventional jump conditions. Furthermore, the findings highlight the significant influence of the selected interface model on the behavior of the system.

infographic.key_insight: A finite element model couples pure fluid flow to a deformable poroelastic medium, showing that interface dissipation can significantly change system behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports simulations of fluid interacting with deformable porous structures where interface assumptions affect predicted responses.
method: Use mixture theory and an arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian formulation for both domains.
Allow discontinuous fluid velocity and pressure while maintaining a globally continuous solid-displacement and mesh-motion field.
Enforce normal filtration-velocity continuity with a Lagrange multiplier and incorporate traction transfer and dissipative momentum jump conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution tests showed satisfactory convergence, an analytical benchmark was reproduced using conventional jump conditions, and a sample problem compared inert and fully dissipative interfaces.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical verification but no experimental validation; selecting an appropriate interface dissipation model remains application-dependent.
infographic.paper_title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface
